That‘s why you, I believe, you were honored. You have played so many different styles.
Right, you know, I certainly…
And you played with so many different people…
I certainly appreciate this…

And you could get along with so many people that you could do all these things. I think that that‘s why Snooky Young has to be recognized because this is important. It‘s not just about being a star; it‘s about this consistent maintenance of excellence and to set
a standard. That‘s why I believe that Snooky Young has made a valuable contribution to American music.

Well, Anthony, I certainly appreciate that and what you‘re saying, it wasn‘t easy to do. And I appreciate you appreciating, or being able to tell me what I have done, or what has been done so far as my musical ability is concerned. It wasn‘t easy by no means, and I just want to thank you for saying these things, what I had been through because I did go through a lot. And at the beginning I was afraid, but I then I grew out of that as I got older, because I went into it as a kid, which is very good. It‘s good too to go in when you‘re very young and if you grow with it, it‘s just like a tree growing from a little plant on up. And if you, you know, if you‘re into it and you like it, I was into music, I come from a musical family, and so…well, that…

Well, against all those odds, against, you know, the country when it was young at the turn of the century in 1919 when you were born. That you then picked up the trumpet at age five and now have been playing the trumpet for eighty-five years, and anybody in the music business when they hear the name Snooky Young, they have a good feeling, they know that that‘s a man of integrity and they know that‘s a man who is a true artist; that's what I believe about Snooky Young.
Well, I certainly appreciate that. I appreciate that so much.

But that‘s what you created, that‘s your career, that was your life. I‘m just trying to see, I‘m just trying to say back to you out of gratitude out of somebody else who participates in this music, as does Ken, that you have set a standard that we all can aspire to because of your creative ability and your humanity, that everyone in this business says that Snooky Young is a man of virtue and a man of integrity, and he can play that trumpet.
Well, I certainly appreciate that and I hope that I have passed some of that on to the younger people who are coming up, I really mean that.
I believe you have Snooky.
I hope I have and I want to thank you for everything actually.

Well, I just want to say we thank you Snooky Young for everything that you‘ve done to give to us, such wonderful music over all these years and that you continue to this day to do what you‘ve been doing for all these years, and that is something very very special.
Thank you. I hope I can continue…

We all hope you will continue… Young:…because it‘s so much fun, to me, to play music. It really is, it‘s a lot of fun to play music, and it‘s kind of tough too, you know. You a musician, so you know what I mean, but I enjoy playing music and I‘m going to continue to play as long as I can.
Thank you Snooky Young.
Thank you.
[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
(Transcribed and edited by Matt Buttermann)

segments.title: Opening of the interview and Snooky Young's birth and name
segments.summary: Brown opens the Smithsonian NEA interview at Young's Los Angeles home; Young confirms his February 3, 1919 birth and that he is Eugene Edward Young, Jr.

segments.title: Parents' origins and the seven Young children
segments.summary: Young gives his father's Dayton roots, his mother's Virginia roots, and names his brothers and sisters.

segments.title: Growing up on Dayton's segregated west side
segments.summary: Young describes the west side as the Black neighborhood and agrees he came up in segregated schools, churches and stores.

segments.title: Dunbar High School and teacher Clarence Francois
segments.summary: Young recalls Dunbar High, its coach Slater and music teacher Clarence Francois, a pianist.

segments.title: Francois puts him on first trumpet; Wilberforce offer and running away
segments.summary: Francois falls out with older brother Granville but puts young Snooky on first trumpet; his mother refuses the Wilberforce offer and he later runs off to join Chick Carter.

segments.title: Father's guitar and banjo, the string family band
segments.summary: Young describes his father teaching his mother guitar and banjo, the uncles in a string group, and his first instrument, the zither.

segments.title: From zither to trumpet and the family dance band
segments.summary: He started on zither, took up trumpet after his brother Granville, a comic performer, and played in the family band with his father on sax and sister Mary Louise on piano.

segments.title: Roy Eldridge sits in at the Cotton Club ballroom
segments.summary: The family band plays Dayton's Cotton Club ballroom, where Roy Eldridge asks to join and the father refuses; Young notes his brother's love of Louis Armstrong.

segments.title: Popular tunes played by the family band
segments.summary: Young recalls the family band played popular tunes such as St. Louis Blues, Stormy Weather and I'm Confessin'.

segments.title: His father as a professional musician with day jobs
segments.summary: His father played alto sax professionally but never left Dayton and held other work as well.

segments.title: A gnat interrupts the interview
segments.summary: Brown and Young swat at a gnat and joke about it.

segments.title: Chick Carter, the singing and dancing bandleader
segments.summary: Chick Carter did not play but sang, danced and conducted like Cab Calloway; the band was small with three trumpets.

segments.title: First trumpet in Carter's band, mouthpieces and playing at ninety
segments.summary: Young replaced Hale, a first trumpeter who kept altering mouthpieces; Young still plays nearly his original mouthpiece and plays with Clayton-Hamilton at ninety.

segments.title: Carter band sidemen and his age when he joined
segments.summary: Young names Tizo Miller, Eddie Berg and Tweedlin' Beard and says he was fifteen or sixteen when he joined.

segments.title: Stranded in New York and a month in a Boston club
segments.summary: The band reached New York but was stranded, never got the Apollo, and played a month in a Boston club.

segments.title: Guessing the violinist who joined Carter's band
segments.summary: Young cannot recall the name of a violin-playing friend who joined the band out of Boston; Brown and Kimery offer wrong guesses.

segments.title: Playing small clubs for about twenty dollars
segments.summary: Young recalls playing steadily in little clubs for eighteen to twenty dollars and bands that never reached the big time.

segments.title: Battle of the bands in Dayton and Gerald Wilson's playing
segments.summary: Carter's last job was a battle against an Alabama college band in Dayton; Gerald Wilson then left for Lunceford, and Young assesses his playing.

segments.title: Replacing Eddie Tompkins in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Gerald Wilson replaced Sy Oliver and Young replaced lead trumpeter Eddie Tompkins, who walked off a Washington stage; Wilson and a Dayton friend of Lunceford's got him the job.

segments.title: Lunceford's difficult, sharp road band and its seven uniforms
segments.summary: Young explains why joining was hard and describes seven uniforms and changing for each of four shows a day.

segments.title: Lunceford pay and relentless one-night stands
segments.summary: Pay was ten dollars a night, a big jump from Chick Carter, with one-nighters five or six days a week.

segments.title: Why the touring big bands trained better musicians
segments.summary: Young laments that today's players lack big-band road schooling and he and Brown list bands like Basie, Hines and Andy Kirk.

segments.title: Ed Saunders and brother Granville with Floyd Ray
segments.summary: Young says a Dayton trumpeter would not join McKinney's Cotton Pickers and his brother went home after Floyd Ray's band.

segments.title: Leaving Lunceford, Lee and Lester Young's band, and Les Hite
segments.summary: Asked about Les Hite, Young says he quit Lunceford in 1942, came west to join the Youngs' band, disliked the small band, and joined Les Hite.

segments.title: First recording and the Uptown Blues solo
segments.summary: His first real recording was with Lunceford, and his solo on Uptown Blues made his name.

segments.title: Being a first trumpet player rather than a soloist
segments.summary: Young says he idolized Roy Eldridge but became a lead player, learned some changes, and soloed little.

segments.title: Other Lunceford solos including Blues in the Night
segments.summary: He confirms soloing on Blues in the Night and recalls solos then were only eight to twelve bars.

segments.title: Why Uptown Blues was given to him and became the theme
segments.summary: Young thinks Lunceford chose him over Wilson and Paul Webster, and the tune became Lunceford's theme song.

segments.title: Dating Uptown Blues to December 1939
segments.summary: Brown reads that it was recorded December 14, 1939; Young works out he joined about three months earlier.

segments.title: Too scared to jam at Minton's in New York
segments.summary: Young describes being a shy nineteen-year-old who would not take his horn out at Minton's while Roy Eldridge hunted for challengers.

segments.title: Influences: Armstrong, Roy Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Young names Armstrong and Eldridge as influences and recalls hanging with Dizzy Gillespie in New York when Gillespie was with Cab Calloway.

segments.title: Leaving Lunceford with Gerald Wilson over a raise
segments.summary: Young and Wilson, the lowest paid men, quit on the bandstand in Detroit after Lunceford refused a raise.

segments.title: Willie Smith, Jimmy Crawford and Dan Grissom
segments.summary: Young praises straw boss Willie Smith and recalls Crawford and singer Dan Grissom.

segments.title: Tape two: how he got the name Snooky
segments.summary: On tape two Young explains that an aunt called him Snooks and that Snooky Young stuck as his professional name.

segments.title: No relation to Lee, Lester or Trummy Young
segments.summary: Young says he is not related to Lee or Lester Young or Trummy Young.

segments.title: Booty Wood and other Dayton musicians
segments.summary: Young recalls Booty Wood as a Dunbar band friend and names Tizo Miller and Lady Bird as other musicians from the Dayton area.

segments.title: Jimmy Crawford, the drummer
segments.summary: Young praises Jimmy Crawford as a beautiful man and great drummer who later worked New York theaters.

segments.title: After Detroit: Dayton, then California and Les Hite
segments.summary: Wilson went to his Dandridge-sister wife in California; Young stayed in Dayton, tried Lee and Lester Young's band, then joined Les Hite with Wilson's help.

segments.title: A month with Basie replacing Buck Clayton
segments.summary: When Basie came through Dayton, Young went on the road for about a month filling in for Buck Clayton.

segments.title: Benny Carter band with a whole trumpet section
segments.summary: With Les Hite slow, Young, Gerald Wilson and two other trumpeters moved together into Benny Carter's band.

segments.title: Short films Blues in the Night and Choo Choo Swing
segments.summary: Brown mentions Young's film shorts; Young does not recall Choo Choo Swing with Basie.

segments.title: Rejoining Basie from 1945 and the dates to the Tonight Show
segments.summary: Brown and Young sort out whether he was with Basie 1945-48 and that he stayed until joining the Tonight Show in 1962.

segments.title: Leading his own group in Dayton with Slam Stewart and Booty Wood
segments.summary: Young confirms he led a group in Dayton with Booty Wood and Slam Stewart in the early 1950s.

segments.title: Opening the Flame Show Bar in Detroit
segments.summary: Young's band opened the Flame Show Bar for eight or ten weeks with star singers like Billie Holiday and Ella Fitzgerald until the union ousted them.

segments.title: Back in Dayton and the club owner's wife
segments.summary: Young returns to Dayton with Slam Stewart, loses the club job when the owner's wife falls for Slam, and goes back to Basie.

segments.title: Family, moving to Long Island and then to California
segments.summary: Young explains his wife and family were in Dayton, he later moved them to Bayside, Long Island, and moved west when the Tonight Show did.

segments.title: Sonny Payne and travelling in his Chrysler Imperial
segments.summary: Young says he and drummer Sonny Payne were close pals who drove between gigs in Payne's Chrysler Imperial.

segments.title: Meeting Thad Jones and the Basie trumpet section
segments.summary: Young first met Thad Jones in Detroit; the Basie section was Thad, Joe Newman, Wendell Culley and Young.

segments.title: Wendell Culley walks off after Marshal Royal hollers
segments.summary: Marshal Royal shouted at Wendell Culley, who nodded out on stage, and Culley packed his horn and was never seen again.

segments.title: Basie as a bandleader, and leaving to join Gerald Wilson's band
segments.summary: Young calls Basie a good boss who let a manager run things; he once left for Gerald Wilson's band, which broke up in St. Louis, and Basie took him back.

segments.title: Replacing Buck Clayton, then playing lead in Basie's trumpet section
segments.summary: Young explains the first stint was a month for Buck Clayton and the later one as first trumpet, with Sweets taking the solos.

segments.title: Developing his cup mute and plunger sound; Clark Terry
segments.summary: Young says he used the cup mute to sound different from open-horn players like Sweets and Joe Newman, and praises Clark Terry's own sound.

segments.title: Louie Bellson's death and plans for the funeral
segments.summary: Young and Brown talk about Louie Bellson's recent death, the funeral arrangements, and Brown's earlier interview with him.

segments.title: Louie Bellson's five-trumpet section and its nicknames
segments.summary: Young recalls playing in Bellson's band, where the five trumpeters had nicknames like Snoo, Blue and Shew, with Bobby Shew on lead.

segments.title: The happy Basie trumpet section of Thad, Joe Newman and Albert Aarons
segments.summary: Young lists the later Basie four-trumpet section and says a section that likes each other plays well.

segments.title: The Atlantic City story of taking Sonny Payne's car keys
segments.summary: Young took the keys of a drunk Sonny Payne's new Imperial; Payne reported it stolen and police stopped Young, a story he tells along with Payne's party habits.

segments.title: Touring by bus, train and car, and the time he and Payne arrived late
segments.summary: Young says Lunceford and Basie travelled by bus and train, Basie disliked flying, and Basie was furious when he and Payne arrived late in Payne's car.

segments.title: Marshal Royal as straw boss and the unnamed white arranger-pianist
segments.summary: Young says Marshal Royal conducted the band and struggles to recall a white California arranger-pianist; a long guessing game over a drummer-led band follows.

segments.title: Personnel on The Atomic Basie and a band with no enemies
segments.summary: Brown reads the 1957 Atomic Basie lineup and Young recalls a friendly band where Basie would call out a flat first half and then the band would light up.

segments.title: Clayton-Hamilton band compared with the Basie band
segments.summary: Young says his current Clayton-Hamilton band has the same spark as the 1957 Basie band.

segments.title: Leaving Basie for the Tonight Show in 1962
segments.summary: Young left Basie because of the Tonight Show offer, urged on by Thad Jones and Frank Wess, and stayed with the show from 1962 to 1992.

segments.title: Tonight Show trumpeters and Bernie Glow
segments.summary: Young recalls Clark Terry, Jimmy Maxwell, Johnny Frosk and first trumpeter Bernie Glow, who wrote an article about him.

segments.title: Cool reception at first in the Tonight Show band
segments.summary: Young says the other musicians did not welcome him at first but Doc Severinsen and Clark Terry were close to him.

segments.title: Tommy Newsom, the square-looking saxophonist and arranger
segments.summary: Young recalls Tommy Newsom, whom Johnny Carson teased, as a sweet man and close friend.

segments.title: Founding member of the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band
segments.summary: Young joined the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band while on the Tonight Show, calls it the best band he played in, and remembers Thad as a close friend and roommate.

segments.title: The Jones brothers and juggling the NBC and Thad-Mel jobs
segments.summary: Young jokes about Elvin and Hank Jones and says there was no conflict between the Tonight Show and the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band, which worked from another studio.

segments.title: Leaving New York for California and liking it
segments.summary: Young says leaving the Thad-Mel band was the hard part of leaving New York and he has always liked California's weather and people.

segments.title: How two-leader bands worked: Thad-Mel and Clayton-Hamilton
segments.summary: Young says co-led bands worked because the leaders respected each other, and recalls Richard Davis in the Thad-Mel rhythm section.

segments.title: Artistic leader versus business leader in co-led bands
segments.summary: Young and Brown agree Thad Jones and John Clayton were the artistic leaders while Mel Lewis and Jeff Hamilton handled business.

segments.title: The Tonight Show moves to Hollywood
segments.summary: Young was happy to follow the show to California, with Doc Severinsen as leader and many friends there.

segments.title: Marrying Dorothy in 1939
segments.summary: Young married his high-school sweetheart Dorothy in 1939 while in Chick Carter's band; they are still together, though she has had a stroke.

segments.title: The Cleveland argument and the letter from a girl
segments.summary: Young tells of a slap from his wife in Cleveland before going on stage and her anger at a letter from a girl.

segments.title: His three children and their music
segments.summary: Young names his daughter Judy, his late son Eugene Edward Young III and a younger daughter, and says his son became a horticulturist; Brown notes his own musician children.

segments.title: Grandchildren
segments.summary: Young talks about his grandchildren, including a grandson who took his trumpet but does not play.

segments.title: Day two opening, February 25, 2009
segments.summary: Brown opens day two at Young's Los Angeles home and asks how he feels.

segments.title: Basie live video from Stockholm, 1962
segments.summary: Brown mentions a 1962 Stockholm video of Basie with Young and plans to show footage later.

segments.title: Sessions with Johnny Hodges and George Benson
segments.summary: Young does not remember a Johnny Hodges session and only vaguely recalls recording with George Benson before he was famous.

segments.title: Oliver Nelson, arranger and friend
segments.summary: Young recalls working with Oliver Nelson in New York, his daughter buying Nelson's house, and later working with him in California.

segments.title: Recording and working with Charles Mingus
segments.summary: Young says he worked and recorded with Mingus, calls his music difficult, and recalls a big-band piece, perhaps Epitaph or the Town Hall concert.

segments.title: Recording with B. B. King
segments.summary: Young says B. B. King called him in to record two or three times.

segments.title: Lifelong friendship with Gerald Wilson
segments.summary: Young says he and Gerald Wilson are as close as ever, and Wilson's college music and collegiate scores helped him become a stronger reader.

segments.title: Never wanting to be a leader; Frank Foster and Basie's later leaders
segments.summary: Young says he never wanted to lead, as with Sweets and Frank Wess, and talks about helping Frank Foster and who led the Basie band afterwards.

segments.title: Eric Dixon
segments.summary: Young recalls tenor saxophonist Eric Dixon as a wonderful man he used to kid.

segments.title: Sonny Cohn and Al Aarons join the trumpet section
segments.summary: Young recalls Sonny Cohn replacing Wendell Culley, who walked off after Marshal Royal's outburst, and Al Aarons arriving.

segments.title: What makes a trumpet section play together
segments.summary: Young says a section works when the players like each other and share advice, and notes how tough the trumpet is.

segments.title: Praise for Sonny Payne and the Basie band
segments.summary: Young and Brown agree Sonny Payne was phenomenal and Young says he loved Basie's band.

segments.title: Hanging with Basie and Lionel Hampton's dinners
segments.summary: Young says he socialised a bit with Basie and tells how Lionel Hampton would invite him to dinner and leave him to pay.

segments.title: Staying young and his daily two-hour practice routine
segments.summary: Young describes practising two hours daily, starting with mouthpiece buzzing, then long tones from a book with a metronome, then playing high notes.

segments.title: Still playing with Gerald Wilson and Clayton-Hamilton
segments.summary: Young says his hearing is weaker but he plays with Wilson and the Clayton-Hamilton band, and he and Wilson came to California within a short time of each other.

segments.title: Tape change; California weather versus Florida and Ohio
segments.summary: After a tape change Young compares Florida and Ohio humidity with California and says why he loves California.

segments.title: Whether he was Doc Severinsen's high-note safety net
segments.summary: Young denies ever covering high notes for Doc Severinsen and says Doc had chops.

segments.title: Covering a note for Dizzy Gillespie and lending him a mouthpiece
segments.summary: Young recalls hitting a high note for Dizzy on one Tonight Show tune and lending Dizzy his mouthpiece in New York.

segments.title: Tonight Show schedule left evenings free for other bands
segments.summary: Young explains the show's rehearsal and one-hour taping left time to play with Thad and Mel in New York and with other bands in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Rehearsing acts quickly with Doc and Tommy Newsom
segments.summary: Young describes the demanding sight-reading of acts' music, Doc and Newsom's rehearsal style, and how Doc Severinsen and Clark Terry helped him in.

segments.title: Tonight Show drummers Ed Shaughnessy and Grady Tate
segments.summary: Young and Brown try to recall the show's drummers; he praises Ed Shaughnessy and his friend Grady Tate.

segments.title: Carson wanted the band to swing more
segments.summary: Young says the band became more jazz-oriented, especially after the move to California, because Carson and Doc wanted jazz players.

segments.title: Johnny Carson and the drums
segments.summary: Young recalls Johnny Carson joking with him and sitting in on drums at rehearsals.

segments.title: Buddy Rich: learning a chart in one hearing
segments.summary: Young recalls Buddy Rich on the Tonight Show, who never read music and played an arrangement after hearing the band play it once, and who was hard on some of his men but not on Young.

segments.title: Louie Bellson's funeral again
segments.summary: Brown and Young again mention Louie Bellson's recent death and the funeral on Thursday.

segments.title: The Tonight Show ends with Carson's departure and what came after
segments.summary: Young says the band left the night Carson did his last show, he was ready with work including the Clayton-Hamilton band, and he did a couple later shows with the new band.

segments.title: Break between tape sessions
segments.summary: Brown calls a break after nearly an hour, noting two more hours to go.

segments.title: Practice, chops and tone advice for young trumpeters
segments.summary: Resuming after a break, Young says daily practice keeps the embouchure and tone in shape and that tone matters more than anything.

segments.title: Whose trumpet tone he admires: Armstrong, Eldridge, Gillespie, Clifford Brown
segments.summary: Asked whom students should hear, Young names the tones of Armstrong, Roy Eldridge, Dizzy Gillespie and Clifford Brown.

segments.title: Freddie Webster
segments.summary: Young says Freddie Webster had a big sound, followed him into Lunceford's band, and died young from bad habits.

segments.title: Fats Navarro
segments.summary: Young remembers Fats Navarro as a great player with range who died young before becoming widely known.

segments.title: Miles Davis
segments.summary: Young says Miles Davis did his own thing, including playing with his horn down, and had it all in his head.

segments.title: Replacing Ed Lewis as Basie's first trumpet
segments.summary: Young says he replaced Ed Lewis, whose age probably ended his time, and that doing so helped put swing into the band.

segments.title: Basie, not Benny Goodman, as the real king of swing
segments.summary: Young argues Basie's band with Jo Jones, Walter Page and Freddie Green swung hardest and that race put Goodman above Basie.

segments.title: Al Killian and the high-note man in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Young remembers Al Killian as a great high-note player who died young, and a Lunceford high-note trumpeter on Rhythm Is Our Business.

segments.title: Declining to talk about Cat Anderson
segments.summary: Asked about Duke Ellington's trumpeters, Young declines to talk about Cat Anderson.

segments.title: The Lunceford trumpeter named Steve before Paul Webster
segments.summary: Young identifies Steve as the high-note trumpeter who played Rhythm Is Our Business before Paul Webster joined.

segments.title: Ellington trumpeters Cootie Williams, Ray Nance and Bubber Miley
segments.summary: Young describes Cootie Williams' side-of-the-mouth playing, Ray Nance's dancing and violin, and Bubber Miley's plunger work.

segments.title: Lee Morgan and his early death
segments.summary: Young says Lee Morgan was on his way to greatness when a woman shot him at Slug's.

segments.title: Woody Shaw
segments.summary: Young knows the name Woody Shaw but not his playing and thinks he would have been well known had he lived.

segments.title: Freddie Hubbard's wild night near Ronnie Scott's in London
segments.summary: Young tells of Freddie Hubbard drunkenly pestering prostitutes on the way to Ronnie Scott's and Young pulling him away.

segments.title: Freddie Hubbard's sound and his needling about the Tonight Show
segments.summary: Young praises Hubbard's beautiful tone, says bad habits ruined his chops, and recalls Hubbard teasing that he could do the Tonight Show job.

segments.title: Getting along with leaders to keep a studio job
segments.summary: Young says musicians are let go from jobs like the Tonight Show for attitude or lateness and he lasted by being on time and easy to work with.

segments.title: Singing T'ain't What You Do at his Tonight Show birthday
segments.summary: Brown mentions a clip of Young singing the Lunceford tune on the Tonight Show; Young says someone arranged it for him.

segments.title: Never getting to sing or dance in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Young says he never got a vocal in Lunceford's band although everyone else sang, and he wished he could sing and dance like Ray Nance.

segments.title: Learning to dance from the Brown Skinned Models show
segments.summary: Young says he learned time steps while the family band toured with a show he thinks was the Brown Skinned Models.

segments.title: Buck-and-wing, hucklebuck and tap dancing
segments.summary: Young says he could do the buck-and-wing, hucklebuck and tap routines with the time step and over-the-top.

segments.title: Friendship with the Nicholas Brothers
segments.summary: Young recalls running with Fayard and Harold Nicholas, who were about his age, after sorting out their names with Brown.

segments.title: Playing with Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham
segments.summary: Young got the Cheathams on the Tonight Show and played in their small blues group with Jeannie on piano and vocals.

segments.title: Trying to name the Cheatham group's drummer, Iron Man
segments.summary: Kimery and Brown try to explain a Detroit drummer nicknamed Iron Man, a name Young cannot hear clearly.

segments.title: The Cheatham group's recordings and Jeannie's stroke
segments.summary: Young recalls the blues group's recordings, learns Jeannie Cheatham has had a stroke, and compares it to his wife's.

segments.title: Duke Ellington's offer and the cold personalities in his band
segments.summary: Duke asked Young to quit Basie and wait two weeks, but Young stayed with Basie and says some of Duke's men turned their backs on each other.

segments.title: Cat Anderson and the borrowed money
segments.summary: Young tells how Cat Anderson borrowed gambling money and refused to repay him.

segments.title: Good young trumpet players today
segments.summary: Young praises young trumpeters in the Clayton-Hamilton band and Winston Bird, and hopes another Louis or Roy comes along.

segments.title: Maynard Ferguson
segments.summary: Young remembers Maynard Ferguson as a nice man, multi-instrumentalist and one of the highest trumpet players ever.

segments.title: Receiving the NEA Jazz Masters award in New York
segments.summary: Young recalls going to New York in the fall to receive the award and the struggle to name fellow recipients.

segments.title: What the NEA award means to a first trumpet player
segments.summary: Young says the honor was nice because it acknowledged the work of a first trumpet player.

segments.title: What a first trumpet player does
segments.summary: Young explains the lead trumpeter leads the section, which follows and blends, and the leading players of each section must think alike.

segments.title: Tape nearly finished and moving to the tour
segments.summary: Brown and Kimery note the tape is almost finished and discuss moving on to the home tour.

segments.title: Young's message for future listeners
segments.summary: Asked what to leave for listeners to the Smithsonian recording, Young says he is honored to be chosen.

segments.title: Brown's tribute to his standard of excellence, and Young's thanks
segments.summary: Brown says Young set a standard of excellence and integrity over eighty-five years; Young thanks him and hopes he has passed it on.

segments.title: Closing thanks and playing as long as he can
segments.summary: Young says playing music is fun and he will continue as long as he can, and the interview ends.
